title: Stage kings and masks
hookLine: the rich are like stage kings: purple outside, poor inside (Letters 80)

lines: A KING IN PURPLE ON THE STAGE.
cards: Everyone who usually bothers Seneca has gone off to watch a public match, and for once nobody knocks on his door. In the quiet, he writes the eightieth letter, and his mind wanders to the theater.
On stage, an actor in a purple robe strides forward and declares he rules over Argos. Another threatens to kill Menelaus with his own hand. Then the play ends, and the kings go home.
Seneca knows exactly what that actor earns, and he thinks the same thing happens on the streets of Rome every day, without a stage.

teach.h: THE KING EARNS A FEW COINS.
teach.b: The man who stalks across the stage saying he rules Argos, Seneca says, is a slave, paid five measures of grain and five denarii. The one threatening Menelaus is paid by the day and sleeps on rags. The purple is costume.
The crown is borrowed. The people carried in litters above the crowd are the same, he says.
His word for their happiness is personata: masked. Take off the mask, and there may be little left to envy.

teach.h: TAKE THE SADDLE OFF THE HORSE.
teach.b: When you buy a horse, Seneca points out, you have the saddle and blanket taken off, so you can see the animal. When you judge a person, don't count the estate, the clothes or the title. Weigh the person, not the wrapping.

teach.h: PERSONA: THE MASK, NOT THE FACE.
teach.b: Persona was the Latin word for an actor's mask, and dictionaries trace our word person back to it. Seneca's point cuts both ways.
Don't be fooled by someone else's mask, and don't confuse your own with your face. The job title, the follower count, the nice car: costumes. Useful sometimes.

how: Readers of Seneca often try to judge others, and themselves, apart from wealth, titles and appearances, the way he says a buyer looks at a horse without its saddle.

o: Latin for an actor's mask, the root of our word person
a well-known Roman actor who played the kings of Argos
the inner self you show only to close friends

games.q: the stage king — tap the pairs.
p: an actor on a small wage

s: the actor playing a king was paid like a king
Seneca says he got five measures of grain and five denarii.
Seneca says to judge a person without their estate and clothes
like taking the saddle off a horse before you buy it.
Seneca wrote the eightieth letter while the crowds were away at a match

games.q: you're buying a horse and the seller has it draped in a gorgeous blanket and saddle. what does Seneca say a buyer does?
o: pay extra for the beautiful blanket.
have the blanket and saddle taken off to see the horse.
games.why: Seneca uses it to say: weigh a person without the estate, the title and the fine clothes.

practice: Think of one person whose life looks enviable to you, and picture their costume: the clothes, the house, the title.
Now imagine them at home after the play, robe off, sitting on the edge of the bed, and let them be a person, not a role. Then take off one piece of your own costume, and breathe as yourself.

wordCard.voice: Persona. The Latin word for an actor's mask, and the root of our word person: don't confuse someone's costume, or your own, with the face beneath. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: an actor's mask; the root of English 'person'.

carryVoice: Your line: behind the mask. Under every costume, a person. Day four hundred seventy-three, done.
